references.text: Just before this verse, it is told that many of the Samaritans believed because of the woman's testimony ([ref:Joh 4:39|John 4:39]). Verse 41 expands on this by saying that even more came to believe because of Jesus' own word – a contrast between indirect and direct testimony.

The following verse ([ref:Joh 4:42|John 4:42]) explains why many more believed: they had now heard Jesus themselves and knew that he is the Savior of the world. This elaborates on the content of the faith mentioned in verse 41.

In his high priestly prayer, Jesus prays that those who come to believe through the disciples' word will also be one ([ref:Joh 17:20|John 17:20]). The principle is the same: faith comes through proclaimed word, just as the Samaritans came to believe through Jesus' own words.

Paul writes that "faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ" ([ref:Rom 10:17|Romans 10:17]). This corresponds with John 4:41, where many more came to believe precisely because of Jesus' own word (τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ).

Also in Jerusalem, many believed in the name of Jesus when they saw the signs he performed ([ref:Joh 2:23|John 2:23]). In contrast to this, the faith in Samaria is based on Jesus' word, not on signs – pointing toward a deeper form of faith in the Gospel of John.

Also on the other side of the Jordan, many came to believe in Jesus ([ref:Joh 10:41-42|John 10:41-42]). The pattern repeats itself: Jesus' word and testimony lead many to believe, even outside Jerusalem.

In Acts it is told that the Samaritans came to believe when Philip preached the gospel to them ([ref:Apg 8:12|Acts 8:12]). This shows a continuation of what began in John 4 – the Samaritans' receptiveness to God's word.

John writes that the signs are recorded so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Messiah ([ref:Joh 20:30-31|John 20:30-31]). The word (λόγος) that leads to faith is a recurring theme in the Gospel of John, and the Samaritans' faith in 4:41 is an early example of this.
